Text: When moving a patient on stairs, {{c1::more than half::how much}} of the patient's weight is distributed to the {{c2::head::head or foot}} end of the carrying device, so the {{c2::strongest}} provider is positioned at that end.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: on a flat stretcher lift, the tallest EMTs take the head end (the stretcher's head end sits slightly higher by design); on stairs the head end is assigned by strength, because the weight shifts to it.

Pitfall: extra hands do not spare the head end; even with four or more providers, head-end strain still increases on a narrow flight of stairs.

Cue: for the stair carry itself the patient rides secured to a backboard, and the wheeled stretcher waits prepared at the bottom.

Text: Carrying a patient up or down a flight of stairs, the two {{c1::strongest}} providers take the head and foot ends. Because of the stairway's incline, if one of the two is considerably taller, it is easier with the {{c2::shorter::taller or shorter}} provider at the head.
Back Extra:
Why: on stairs the device angles with the incline, and proportionally greater weight also lands on the foot-end provider, so both end positions need strength.

Distinguish: tallest-at-head offsets the stretcher's built-in head height on a flat lift; on a stairway the incline is what matters, and the shorter of the two strongest takes the head.
